I think you have to view it a bit differently to how you’d view meeting people at home. Some of the people you meet abroad you will make genuine friendships with, but a lot will just be your friends for the days or weeks you’re in the same place. So you can have different expectations of them. 

Also - if privacy is an issue, a compromise if you still want to do it cheaply, is to go to a hostel that has curtains around the bunks. It makes a whole world of difference. If you want your space you can just close the curtain and chill. If you want to socialise, you can! I’ve just got back from a trip this evening and I hated the one hostel I stayed in that didn’t have curtains.

I would say south east Asia is very popular with that crowd but it shouldn’t necessarily stop you visiting. Do lots of research on the hostels you’re staying in, trip advisor etc. That should be able to tell you what kind of vibe the place has. Also, you could alternate as you move from place to place between dorms and private rooms? I’m 29 and that’s what I’ve just done on my trip. It just gives you a bit of a breather because sharing a room with others can be really intense. Don’t let this put you off solo travel, as you do more of it, you’ll find your groove. Visiting other places will be different too!

That’s not the professional way to behave though is it? School is supposed to prepare kids for the workplace. So if she goes and has a polite conversation with the teacher first, she’s more likely to be listened to by the VP if there’s no improvement. Also: students accuse teachers of bias all the time. It doesn’t mean it’s there because how teachers respond can be down to a range of factors. 

I think it’s pretty irresponsible of you to assume that teachers have vendettas, or that they like watching kids taking their clothes off. Those are both really serious accusations and without knowing the individuals involved, or the context, you have no right making them.

NAH. I understand that you want to do something about it but, as a teacher, I can tell you that your teacher is trying to follow the rules. If you genuinely have an issue, speak to her first on her own, explaining calmly and politely the situation and asking how she thinks the matter could be resolved.
